z→l⊕h→i,j−1+z→t⊕h→i−1,j⊕z→d⊕h→i−1,j−1+z→i⊕h→~i​j,\displaystyle\vec{z}_{l}\oplus\vec{h}_{i,j-1}+\vec{z}_{t}\oplus\vec{h}_{i-1,j}\oplus\vec{z}_{d}\oplus\vec{h}_{i-1,j-1}+\vec{z}_{i}\oplus\tilde{\vec{h}}_{ij}, (60) where q→=[h→i−1,j,h→i,j−1,h→i−1,j−1,x→i​j]T\vec{q}=[\vec{h}_{i-1,j},\vec{h}_{i,j-1},\vec{h}_{i-1,j-1},\vec{x}_{ij}]^{T} is the concatenated vector containing the 3 previous hidden states h→i−1,j,h→i,j−1,h→i−1,j−1\vec{h}_{i-1,j},\vec{h}_{i,j-1},\vec{h}_{i-1,j-1} and the input vector x→i​j\vec{x}_{ij}, r→l,t,d\vec{r}_{l,t,d} are the three reset gates corresponding to h→i,j−1\vec{h}_{i,j-1}, h→i−1,j\vec{h}_{i-1,j}, h→i−1,j−1\vec{h}_{i-1,j-1}, z→l,t,d,i\vec{z}_{l,t,d,i} are the four update gates. The W→\vec{W}’s, U→\vec{U}’s and b→\vec{b}’s are the weight matrices and bias vectors. σ{\sigma} is the sigmoid function, ff is a nonlinear activation function, e.g. tanh\tanh. Even if we were to do away with the hidden state h→i−1,j−1\vec{h}_{i-1,j-1}2525 25 The hidden state h→i−1,j−1\vec{h}_{i-1,j-1} might not be necessary in the context of 2D spin lattice with only vertical and horizontal nearest-neighbor interactions. In their construction of the 2D RNN, the authors of [9] also did not make use of h→i−1,j−1\vec{h}_{i-1,j-1}, see Eq.63., we would still require two reset gates and three update gates for the 2D GRU. As such, with the many more parameters involved in the construction of the 2D Euclidean GRU and the already-complex definitions of various arithmetic operations in hyperbolic space, the hyperbolic 2D GRU (obtained from converting the 2D Euclidean GRU) will necessarily be much more mathematically complex than the 1D hyperbolic GRU. Such a network will be very computationally costly to train, both in terms of time and the hardware resources required.

5.4 1D Heisenberg J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} Model

The Hamiltonian of the one-dimensional Heisenberg J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model is

HJ1​J2​J3=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩Si.Sj+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩Si.Sj+J3​∑⟨⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩⟩Si.Sj\displaystyle H_{J_{1}J_{2}J_{3}}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}S_{i}\,.\,S_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}S_{i}\,.\,S_{j}+J_{3}\sum_{\langle\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle\rangle}S_{i}\,.\,S_{j} (61)

where Si=Sx,Sy,SzS_{i}=S_{x},S_{y},S_{z} are the spin-half operators (Pauli matrices). The first sum with the coefficient J1J_{1} in the Hamiltonian is over pairs of nearest neighbors, the second sum with the coefficient J2J_{2} is over pairs of second nearest neighbors, and the third sum with the coefficient J3J_{3} is over pairs of third nearest neighbors. When both J2≠0J_{2}\neq 0 and J3≠0J_{3}\neq 0, this model has a complicated phase transition properties that depend almost entirely on the relative strength of the competing J2J_{2} and J3J_{3} interactions [54]. Compared to the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model, the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model is studied much less frequently in the literature, and even more so for the case of the one-dimensional J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model, but it is believed that the J3J_{3} interactions in the 1D model between third nearest neighbors are relevant for describing the magnetic properties of quasi one-dimensional edge-shared cuprates such as LiVCuO4 or LiCu2O2 [54].

5.4.1 Experiment details

For the 1D Heisenberg J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model with open boundary condition, we will carry out the VMC experiments with the number of spins N=30N=30 using the following four settings (with J1=1.0J_{1}=1.0):

  1. 1.

    (J2,J3)=(0.0,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0,0.5): No second neighbor interactions, the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model reduces to J1​J3J_{1}J_{3} model with only first and third nearest neighbor interactions.

  2. 2.

    (J2,J3)=(0.2,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.2): Second and third neighbor interactions have the same strength.

  3. 3.

    (J2,J3)=(0.2,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.5): Second neighbor interactions are stronger than third neighbor interactions.

  4. 4.

    (J2,J3)=(0.5,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.5,0.2): Second neighbor interactions are weaker than third neighbor interactions.

The NQS used are the complex Euclidean GRU and hyperbolic GRU ansatzes as in the 1D J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case. We will perform two different sets of VMC experiments.

  • •

    In the first set of experiments, all four (J2,J3J_{2},J_{3}) cases listed above are considered, with the Euclidean/hyperbolic GRU NQS ansatzes used having the same RNN hidden dimension of dh=50d_{h}=50 (see Table 7 for the variant names and their numbers of parameters).

  • •

    In the second set of experiments, we only considered (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3}) = (0.2, 0.5), (0.5, 0.2), with the Euclidean GRU ansatz having the RNN hidden dimension dh=60d_{h}=60. We experimented with various hyperbolic GRU ansatzes, each one having a different dhd_{h} where 53≤dh≤5853\leq d_{h}\leq 58 in order to choose the best performing ansatz to compare the Euclidean NQS (see Table 8).

In the first set of VMC experiments, we only used one variant each for either Euclidean (eGRU-50-s50 with dh=50d_{h}=50) or hyperbolic GRU (hGRU-50-s50 with dh=50d_{h}=50) and fixed the number of training epochs to 280 in all cases. In the second set of VMC experiments, we explored the performances of hyperbolic GRU variants with 53≤dh≤5853\leq d_{h}\leq 58 to choose the best one among them to compare with the Euclidean GRU benchmark, eGRU-60-s50 with dh=60d_{h}=60, while extending the number of training epochs to 450 for (J2,J3)=(0.2,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.5) and 500 for (J2,J3)=(0.5,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.5,0.2). Similar to previous cases, in each experiment, hyperbolic GRU can take up to around 5 times longer to complete the training (on the same hardware) than Euclidean GRU with the same dhd_{h}2626 26 while hyperbolic GRU with smaller dhd_{h} also takes longer to train, up to around 2-3 times, than Euclidean GRU with larger dhd_{h}. All other training details (optimizer settings, saving-of-best-model-only method) remain the same as in the 1D J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case and will not be repeated here.

5.4.2 Results

  • •

    For the first set of VMC experiments involving (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3}) = (0.0, 0.5), (0.2, 0.2), (0.2, 0.5), (0.5, 0.2) with the NQS ansatzes listed in Table 7, the inference results using 10410^{4} samples are listed in Table 9, respectively. Fig.7 graphically shows the data in both these Tables and offers a comparison between the performances of the 1D Euclidean and 1D hyperbolic GRU. The convergence curve plots for the mean energy recorded during the training process are shown in Fig.18 in Appendix B.4.

    From Table 9 and Fig.7, we note that hyperbolic GRU definitively outperformed Euclidean GRU (by a large margin) in all 4 out of 4 cases. The energy convergence curves (see Fig.18) corresponding to the hyperbolic GRU ansatz reach convergence at values well below that reached by the curves corresponding to the Euclidean GRU ansatz.

  • •

    For the second set of VMC experiments involving only (OPENJ2,J3)=(0.2,0.5),(0.5,0.2)J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.5),(0.5,0.2) with the NQS ansatzes listed in Table 8, the inference results are included in Table 10. The comparison of the performances of hyperbolic and Euclidean GRU ansatzes is shown in Fig.8. The convergence curve plots of the second set of VMC experiments for the mean energy recorded during the training process are shown in Fig.19 in Appendix B.4.

    1. 1.

      For (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3}) = (0.2, 0.5), the hyperbolic GRU ansatz hGRU-55-s50, with 9794 parameters, shows an overall comparable performance to the Euclidean GRU ansatz eGRU-60-s50 with 11584 parameters. Although the larger Euclidean GRU ansatz emerges as the better performer by a slight margin, it also has 20 percent more parameters than the hyperbolic GRU network. Furthermore, it is noteworthy to point out that in the training process, hGRU-55-s50 performed better than eGRU-60-s50, as is evident from the energy convergence curve shown in the first subfigure of Fig.19, which shows the curve corresponding to hGRU-55-s50 reaching convergence faster with a narrower fluctuation range than the curve corresponding to eGRU-60-s50.

    2. 2.

      For (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3}) = (0.5, 0.2), the hyperbolic GRU ansatz hGRU-57-s50 outperforms the Euclidean GRU ansatz eGRU-60-s50. In this case, hyperbolic GRU has 10 percent fewer parameters than Euclidean GRU (10492 versus 11584).

From the two sets of VMC experiments for the 1D J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model, we observe that the obtained results showing that hyperbolic GRU almost always outperformed Euclidean GRU are in agreement with the ones in the 1D J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case in which hyperbolic GRU outperfomed its Euclidean version in all cases when J2≠0J_{2}\neq 0, i.e. when the second neighbor interaction is nonvanishing and the Hamiltonian exhibits a hierarchy in the interaction structure comprised of the first and second neighbor interactions. In all four J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} settings where there exist an even more pronounced hierarchy in the interaction structure of the Hamiltonian that comprises the first, second and third nearest neighbor interactions, the clear outperformance of the hyperbolic GRU ansatz reinforces the hypothesis that the hyperbolic geometry of this neural network plays a determining role in handling the type of Hamiltonians with hierarchical structures such as the 1D J1​J2J_{1}J_{2}, J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} systems. As already noted in the 1D J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case (see Section 5.3.2), an interesting task would be to verify whether hyperbolic GRU carries on outperforming Euclidean GRU for the 2D J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} models on different lattice geometries, but this will require the generalization of the 1D hyperbolic GRU network to a 2D version, similar to the generalization of the 1D Euclidean RNN cell to the 2D version in Eq.63 as done in [9]. As also noted in Section 5.3.2, this generalization is a challenging task, given that the complexity of the resulting 2D hyperbolic network will result in training processes that are highly computationally demanding.

6 Concluding remarks

In this work, we introduce the hyperbolic GRU as the first type of non-Euclidean neural quantum state (NQS) to be used in the variational Monte Carlo method (VMC) to approximate the ground state energy in quantum many-body physics, which are represented by the prototypical settings of the one-dimensional & two-dimensional transverse field Ising model (1D/2D TFIM) and the one-dimensional Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} & J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} models. Our results show an interesting trend regarding the performance of the hyperbolic GRU as benchmarked against the performances of its Euclidean counterpart. In particular, from the obtained results of the experiments performed in this work, we note the following.

  • •

    In the 1D TFIM setting, with the number of spins NN being 20, 40, 80 and 100, where the Hamiltonian comprises only the nearest neighbor interaction and a transverse magnetic field, with no hierarchical interaction structure, hyperbolic GRU showed a comparable performance to Euclidean GRU, with both GRU variants outperforming the Euclidean RNN variant.

  • •

    In the 2D TFIM setting, with the number of size of the 2D square lattice (Nx,Ny)(N_{x},N_{y}) being (5,5),(7,7),(8,8)(5,5),(7,7),(8,8), (9,9)(9,9) corresponding to N=25,49,64,81N=25,49,64,81 spins, where the Hamitonian comprises the horizontal and vertical nearest neighbor interaction in two dimensions and a transverse magnetic field, 1D hyperbolic GRU always outperformed 1D Euclidean GRU (while the best performing ansatz, the 2D Euclidean RNN NQS, was included purely to provide a benchmark). In this case, due to the artificial rearrangement or reshaping/folding of the 1D spin chain to mimic the 2D lattice, a hierarchy in the interaction structure, comprising the first and the Nt​hN^{th} nearest neighbor interactions, is introduced when originally faraway spins (at site ii and site i+Ni+N) in the 1D chains become immediate vertical neighbors. The fact that the hyperbolic GRU NQS ansatz outperformed the Euclidean GRU NQS ansatz for this setting is our first clue of the role played by the hyperbolic geometry of the neural network in determining its performance when there is a hierarchical structure in the Hamiltonian.

  • •

    In the 1D Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} setting with N=50N=50 spins, J1=1.0J_{1}=1.0 (fixed) and J2=0.0,0.2,0.5,0.8J_{2}=0.0,0.2,0.5,0.8, hyperbolic GRU definitively outperformed Euclidean GRU when the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} Hamiltonian exhibits a hierarchical interaction structure - when J2≠0J_{2}\neq 0, which takes into account the second nearest neighbor interactions in addition to the first nearest neighbor interactions. This is our second clue of the role played by the hyperbolic geometry of the neural network.

  • •

    In the 1D Heisenberg J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} setting with N=30N=30 spins, J1=1.0J_{1}=1.0 (fixed) and (J2,J3)=(0.0,0.5),(0.2,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0,0.5),(0.2,0.2), (0.2,0.5)(0.2,0.5), (0.5,0.2)(0.5,0.2), hyperbolic GRU again definitively outperformed Euclidean GRU in four out of four cases in the first set of experiments (where the networks have the same number of parameters). In the second set of experiments (involving only the two cases J2=(0.2,0.5)J_{2}=(0.2,0.5) and J2=(0.5,0.2)J_{2}=(0.5,0.2)), where the hyperbolic GRU network has around 10-20 percent fewer parameters than the Euclidean GRU network, hyperbolic GRU attained a comparable performance with Euclidean GRU in one case and outperformed Euclidean GRU in another case. In this setting, the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} Hamiltonian exhibits even more pronounced hierarchical interaction structures comprising the first, second and third nearest neighbors. This is our third clue.

At this point, it is useful to recall the established results in natural language processing (NLP) and graph embedding that hyperbolic RNNs almost always outperform their Euclidean versions when the training data exhibit hierarchical structures [30], [36], [34]. In these NLP/graph embedding contexts, the fact that hierarchical structures are often tree-like in nature largely explains the superior performances of hyperbolic neural networks, since a key property of hyperbolic space - the exponential expansion of space at large distances - is responsible for its ability to accomodate or embed tree structures with very low distortions. In the context of physical Hamiltonian spin systems, the hierarchical structures are not really tree-like in nature, but nonetheless a clear hierarchy in the interaction part exists in all the systems that hyperbolic NQS was found to have outperformed its Euclidean counterpart. Thus, it is our hypothesis that hyperbolic RNN-based NQS will likely outperform Euclidean RNN-based NQS in all quantum spin systems in which there is a hierarchical structure in the interaction part of the Hamiltonian. Given the fact that the experiments done in this work have only involved small-size systems due to our limited computing resources, it is obvious that more works are needed to either confirm or refute this hypothesis. If true, this would be an exciting new direction opened up by the possibility of better performances delivered hyperbolic and potentially other non-Euclidean NQS in the problem of approximating the ground state energy of quantum many-body Hamiltonians using VMC - a problem that has been studied using exclusively conventional or Euclidean neural networks.

Several interesting generalizations exist given the results of this work.

  • •

    One immediate and specific direction involves the generalization of the one-dimensional hyperbolic GRU NQS in this work to two dimensions, and compare the performance of this 2D hyperbolic GRU against the 2D Euclidean GRU in the settings of 2D TFIM or 2D Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} and J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} models. The main challenge for this task lies in the fact that the computational cost required to train the 2D Euclidean and hyperbolic GRUs will be much more intensive than the already-intensive computational cost required to train the 1D hyperbolic GRU. This is because given the fact that the 2D Euclidean GRU is more mathematically complex than the 1D GRU, its hyperbolic conversion will necessarily result in an even more complex construction, as previously noted in detail in Section 5.3.2.

  • •

    Other broader directions involve the exploration of a different type of hyperbolic RNNs, for example one that is based on the Lorentz model of hyperbolic space [32], [33] instead of the Poincaré model, in various quantum many-body settings. It is known that hyperbolic networks based on the Lorentz model exhibit a more stable behavior compared to those based on the Poincaré model during the training process2727 27 In the Poincaré model, the metric includes a term 2/(1−‖x‖2)2/(1-||x||^{2}) (see Eq.9), which causes a ‘singularity’ at the boundary, or in other words, the distance grows to infinity at the edge of the Poincaré ball. During the training process, a small update in the vicinity of the boundary can lead to a very large change in the hyperbolic distance and subsequently a gradient explosion problem. On the other hand, the Lorentz model of DD-dimensional hyperbolic space does not have a singularity in its metric, since it is defined as a DD-dimensional hypersurface ℋD\mathcal{H}^{D} in (D+1)(D+1) dimensional Euclidean space ℝD+1\mathbb{R}^{D+1}: ℋD={x→∈ℝD+1:⟨x→,x→⟩=−1,x0>0},where⟨x→,y→⟩=−x0y0+∑i=1Dxiyi.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{D}=\left\{\vec{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{D+1}:\langle\vec{x},\vec{x}\rangle=-1,x_{0}>0\right\},\hskip 11.38109pt\text{where}\hskip 8.53581pt\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle=-x_{0}y_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{D}x_{i}y_{i}\,. (62) The distance function in ℋD\mathcal{H}^{D} is d⁡(x→,y→)=arccosh​(−⟨x→,y→⟩)d(\vec{x},\vec{y})=\text{arccosh}\left(-\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle\right), which does not have a singularity. , and this is especially the case with larger or deeper hyperbolic networks [32]. With the increasing sizes of the quantum systems of interest, it might be more suitable to switch from Poincaré-based hyperbolic networks to the Lorentz-based hyperbolic ones for precisely this reason.

  • •

    Yet even more general directions involve the explorations of different types of non-Euclidean NQS beyond hyperbolic RNNs. These new types of non-Euclidean NQS could include, for example, the hyperbolic CNN networks [37] or the hyperbolic transformer neural network [33].

We leave these issues to future works.

Appendix A Two-dimensional RNN model

The 2D Euclidean RNN is a new custom construction from [9] with the following defining equation2828 28 A more general discussion of the multi-dimensional RNN can be found in [55].

h→t+1=f⁡(Uh​x→t0+Wh​h→t0+Uv​x→t1+Wv​h→t0+b→),\displaystyle\vec{h}_{t+1}=f\left(U_{h}\vec{x}^{0}_{t}+W_{h}\vec{h}^{0}_{t}+U_{v}\vec{x}^{1}_{t}+W_{v}\vec{h}_{t}^{0}+\vec{b}\right)\,, (63)

where ff is a nonlinear activation function, the input x→t=(x→t0,x→t1)\vec{x}_{t}=(\vec{x}^{0}_{t},\vec{x}^{1}_{t}) and hidden state h→t=(h→t0,h→t1)\vec{h}_{t}=(\vec{h}^{0}_{t},\vec{h}^{1}_{t}) at timestep tt are now a 2D vectors comprising the horizontal and vertical components. Correspondingly, there is a doubling of the ususal weight matrices UU and WW to Uh,UvU_{h},U_{v}, Wh,WvW_{h},W_{v}. For a 2D spin configuration σ\mathbf{{\sigma}} of dimension (Nx,NyCLOSE(N_{x},N_{y}), an entry σi,j{\sigma}_{i,j} is autoregressively generated based on the two spins and two hidden states from its previously generated horizontal and vertical neighbors. For the 1D Euclidean/hyperbolic GRU, during the sampling process, the site σi,j{\sigma}_{i,j} is autoregressively generated based on only the previously generated site in a raster manner shown in Fig.9. At each time step tt during the training phase, the 2D Euclidean RNN NQS ansatz generates 50 two-dimensional samples, each of which is a (2D) spin configuration (samples) of size (Nx,NyCLOSE(N_{x},N_{y}), while the 1D Euclidean/hyperbolic GRU ansatz generates 50 one-dimensional samples, each of which is a (1D) spin configuration of length Nx×NyN_{x}\times N_{y}. The computation of the energy for the 1D ansatz requires a reshaping of the 1D samples of length Nx×NyN_{x}\times N_{y} into 2D samples of size (Nx,Ny)(N_{x},N_{y}).

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
